title: Observable systems with divergent isolated Kalman covariances
shortTitle: Kalman filter shortcut: reported uncertainty can explode
oneLine: A three-unit example, observable and controllable, makes the isolated Kalman filter's reported variances grow at least like (5/4)(9/5)^k while the ordinary Kalman filter stays at or below 3/4, refuting its authors' conjecture that the reported covariance always settles to a unique steady state.
abstract: Teams of robots or sensors often share the work of tracking a common state. The isolated Kalman filter of Jung, Luft and Weiss (Autonomous Robots, 2025) saves communication by updating only the units involved in each measurement and approximating their links to everyone else with a correction factor. Its authors conjectured that, whenever the system is observable and controllable, the covariance the filter reports settles to a finite, unique, stable steady state. This candidate shows that the conjecture is false. In a three-unit system where each measurement sees the sum of two states, observable from one round of measurements and controllable, with every local update well defined, the reported variances are proved to satisfy m_k ≥ (5/4)(9/5)^k − 1/4 for dynamics A = 3I, while the centralised Kalman filter keeps every variance at most 3/4. A Perron-root criterion extends the divergence to every connected non-bipartite graph of pair-sum measurements, and extra attenuation or deletion of cross-covariances does not help. Divergence needs unstable dynamics (stable dynamics are proved bounded), but only mildly: computer-assisted interval-arithmetic proofs show that large priors escape for growth factors a² in (1, 1.38], with certified entry from 10¹²I at eight values down to 1 + 10⁻⁸, and that at a² = 21/20 the prior I settles while 10¹²I diverges, so no steady covariance attracts every start. In high-precision numerical tests the actual estimation error stays bounded: the failure is gross pessimism of the reported covariance, not divergence of the estimate. The paper also classifies when every local update is well defined (participant groups overlapping in at most one unit) and proves boundedness for anchored relative measurements. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Counterexample (Theorem 4.1): three scalar nodes observed through x₁+x₂, x₂+x₃, x₃+x₁ with A = 3I, Q = R = P₀ = I are observable from one epoch and controllable, every local block stays positive definite, yet the smallest reported IsoKF variance satisfies m_k ≥ (5/4)(9/5)^k − 1/4 → ∞, while the centralised Kalman filter keeps every variance at most 3/4.

Graph criterion (Theorem 5.1, Corollary 5.3): every connected non-bipartite pair-sum graph diverges once a² reaches the Perron root of a schedule matrix (2+√5 ≈ 4.236 for the triangle); further attenuation, including deleting cross-covariances, does not restore boundedness.

Mild instability and non-uniqueness (Theorems 6.2, 6.4, Corollaries 6.3, 6.5; computer-assisted): for a² in (1, 1.38] large priors diverge at rate a^(2k) once in a certified region, entered from 10¹²I at eight values down to a² = 1 + 10⁻⁸; at a² = 21/20 the prior I converges while 10¹²I diverges, so there is no globally attracting steady covariance.

Meaning (Findings 7.1-7.2; numerical): in the tested divergent cases the actual error of the IsoKF estimate stays bounded, so the failure is gross pessimism of the reported covariance; the divergence threshold from P₀ = I is near a² ≈ 1.1225, far below the deletion variant's threshold close to 2+√5.

Safe regimes (Proposition 3.1, Theorem 8.1, Proposition 9.1): Schur-stable dynamics give bounded marginals; local blocks always stay positive definite exactly when participant groups share at most one node; anchored full-coordinate relative measurements stay bounded.

narration: Can a team of robots trust the uncertainty it reports? An Evidence Press briefing. When several robots or sensors track a shared state, an ordinary Kalman filter would keep one large table of how uncertain every quantity is and how the errors are linked. Sending that table around is expensive. The isolated Kalman filter, published by Jung, Luft and Weiss in Autonomous Robots in 2025, saves communication. When a measurement involves a few units, only those units update properly, and their links to everyone else are approximated by a simple correction. Its authors conjectured that, whenever the system can be observed and controlled, the uncertainty this filter reports always settles to one finite, stable value. This paper shows that it does not. Take three units, and let each measurement see the sum of two of their states. The system is observable and controllable, and every local step of the filter stays valid. Yet with states that triple at every step, the reported variances grow without limit: they are proved to be at least five quarters times nine fifths to the power k, minus one quarter, after k rounds. The ordinary, centralised Kalman filter on the same system keeps every variance at or below three quarters. The failure also appears with much milder growth. Computer-assisted proofs show that large starting uncertainty escapes when the growth per step is only slightly above one, and that at one growth rate a small start settles while a large start explodes, so no single steady value attracts every start. There are honest limits. In the tests, the filter's actual error stayed bounded; what fails is the reported uncertainty, which becomes wildly pessimistic and stops meaning anything. Stable systems are proved never to diverge, and anchored relative measurements stay safe. This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review only. This narration uses a synthetic voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Jung, Luft and Weiss (2025). Isolated Kalman filtering: theory and decoupled estimator design. Autonomous Robots. Introduces the isolated Kalman filter, its update equations (47)-(50) and the convergence conjecture refuted here.

Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2016). Recursive Decentralized Collaborative Localization for Sparsely Communicating Robots. Robotics: Science and Systems XII. Origin of the marginal-ratio cross-covariance correction.

Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2018). Recursive decentralized localization for multi-robot systems with asynchronous pairwise communication. The International Journal of Robotics Research. Journal version of the correction (eq. 26), with a scaled variant (eq. 28) and a proof that two-robot blocks stay positive definite (Proposition 1); read in full. It makes no claim about boundedness or convergence of the covariance and gives no divergence example.
Roumeliotis and Bekey (2002). Distributed multirobot localization. IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation. Decomposed centralised filtering for collaborative localization.
Schmidt (1966). Application of State-Space Methods to Navigation Problems. Advances in Control Systems. The consider (Schmidt) filter, which also updates only some states.

Julier and Uhlmann (1997). A non-divergent estimation algorithm in the presence of unknown correlations. Proceedings of the 1997 American Control Conference. Covariance intersection, a conservative alternative for unknown correlations.

Li and Nashashibi (2012). Cooperative multi-vehicle localization using split covariance intersection filter. 2012 IEEE Intelligent Vehicles Symposium. Split covariance intersection for cooperative localization.

Chan, Goodwin and Sin (1984). Convergence properties of the Riccati difference equation in optimal filtering of nonstabilizable systems. IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control. Classical Riccati convergence theory used for the centralised comparison.
Weiss and Freeman (2001). Correctness of Belief Propagation in Gaussian Graphical Models of Arbitrary Topology. Neural Computation. Odd-cycle phenomena in another local covariance recursion.

Georgescu, Higham and Peters (2018). Explicit solutions to correlation matrix completion problems, with an application to risk management and insurance. Royal Society Open Science. Matrix completion background for globally consistent covariance arrays.

De Carli and Dimarogonas (2025). A Distributed Kalman-Like Observer With Dynamic Inversion-Based Correction for Multi-Agent Estimation. IEEE Control Systems Letters. A citing work checked in the forward-citation sweep.
Jung (2024). Recursive Distributed Collaborative Aided Inertial Navigation. PhD thesis, arXiv:2408.12360. Dissertation formulation of the conjecture.

decisionObject.description: Whether the isolated Kalman filter's reported covariance converges to a finite, unique, stable steady state for every completely observable and controllable system (the Jung-Luft-Weiss conjecture): no.
decisionObject.scope: Linear time-invariant systems with the published IsoKF update; the counterexamples use pair-sum observation channels and unstable (possibly very mildly unstable) dynamics; stable dynamics are proved bounded.

corrections.summary: Corrected the comparison with Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2018, IJRR). Version 0.1.0 compared the work with that article at abstract level only. Version 0.2.0 compares it with the full text: it introduces the correction factor (eq. 26) and a scaled variant (eq. 28), proves that two-robot blocks stay positive definite (Proposition 1), and makes no claim about boundedness or convergence of the covariance and gives no divergence example. Its Proposition 1 and scaled variant are now credited where our results overlap, and the two citing works are compared in full text.
